clinicalPearls: Results from a lesion of the dorsal caudal pontine tegmentum in the paramedian basilar territory
Combines an ipsilateral conjugate horizontal gaze palsy with ipsilateral facial weakness and contralateral hemiparesis
The gaze palsy reflects involvement of the abducens nucleus and paramedian pontine reticular formation, so both eyes fail to look towards the lesion
Ipsilateral lower motor neurone facial weakness follows involvement of the facial nucleus or its looping fibres around the abducens nucleus
Contralateral limb weakness arises from corticospinal fibres, giving another caudal alternating hemiplegia
It differs from Millard-Gubler syndrome chiefly by the conjugate gaze palsy rather than an isolated abduction deficit
An ipsilateral Horner syndrome or facial sensory loss may occur if the lesion extends laterally
reference.pathophysiology: Foville syndrome follows a dorsal caudal pontine tegmental lesion supplied by paramedian branches of the basilar artery. The infarct involves the abducens nucleus and the neighbouring paramedian pontine reticular formation, disrupting conjugate horizontal gaze towards the side of the lesion, and the genu of the facial nerve looping around the abducens nucleus, producing ipsilateral lower motor neurone facial weakness. Extension ventrally to the corticospinal fibres in the basis pontis produces contralateral limb weakness. The involvement of the gaze centre rather than the isolated sixth nerve fascicle distinguishes it from Millard-Gubler syndrome, while both share the crossed facial and limb pattern.
additionalDifferentials: One-and-a-half syndrome from dorsal pontine lesions
Hemispheric lesion causing a contralateral gaze preference
Basilar artery thrombosis with brainstem signs
additionalInvestigations: Diffusion-weighted MRI of the dorsal caudal pons to localise the lesion
MR or CT angiography of the basilar artery and posterior circulation
Detailed assessment of conjugate horizontal gaze and vestibulo-ocular reflexes
Facial nerve examination distinguishing upper from lower motor neurone weakness
Cardiovascular and stroke risk workup including ECG and metabolic profiling
Vessel wall imaging where basilar atherosclerosis or dissection is suspected
redFlags: Progressive drowsiness or quadriparesis suggesting evolving basilar thrombosis
Bilateral pontine signs raising the possibility of a locked-in state
Expanding deficit indicating a pontine haemorrhage
New respiratory or bulbar compromise from brainstem extension
reference.prognosis: Limited dorsal pontine infarcts may recover useful gaze and limb function, but the horizontal gaze palsy can persist, and lesions signalling basilar disease carry the risk of progression and a poorer outcome.
pitfalls: Confusing the ipsilateral gaze palsy with a hemispheric contralateral gaze deviation
Mistaking Foville for Millard-Gubler by overlooking the conjugate nature of the gaze defect
Attributing the facial weakness to a peripheral Bell palsy in isolation
Missing an evolving basilar occlusion behind seemingly focal pontine signs
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Deliver hyperacute stroke reperfusion — intravenous thrombolysis or, for basilar and posterior-circulation occlusion, mechanical thrombectomy — where the patient is eligible
Establish secondary prevention with antiplatelet or, for cardioembolic or dissection-related stroke, anticoagulant therapy, plus a statin and vascular risk-factor control
Monitor closely for basilar-territory progression, with critical-care support given the risk of brainstem deterioration
Protect the eye and manage diplopia from the gaze palsy and facial weakness with lubrication, prisms or occlusion
Assess swallowing and protect the airway to prevent aspiration
Provide multidisciplinary neurorehabilitation with physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy
Investigate and treat the vascular cause, such as basilar atherosclerosis or dissection, through a stroke service

nodes.text: Suspected Foville syndrome: ipsilateral conjugate gaze palsy with facial weakness
Red flag present (drowsiness, quadriparesis, bilateral pontine signs)?
Urgent stroke pathway: evolving basilar thrombosis or pontine haemorrhage
Diffusion-weighted MRI and CT or MR angiography of the basilar artery
Does diffusion MRI localise a dorsal caudal pontine lesion?
Consider Millard-Gubler syndrome, one-and-a-half syndrome or a hemispheric lesion
Hyperacute reperfusion with thrombolysis or thrombectomy where eligible
Antiplatelet, or anticoagulant if cardioembolic, plus statin
Neurorehabilitation with physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy
